opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a tricky comparison, and people often get it wrong in both directions.

On one hand, evolution had an enormous amount of "compute" to work with. You're talking about billions of years and astronomical numbers of organisms, each one effectively an experiment. So when people say "look how efficient the brain is" or "look how elegant a bird's flight is," and conclude that engineering is hopelessly behind, they're comparing a few decades of human effort against a search process that ran on a planetary scale for an absurdly long time. Measured that way, humans look remarkably fast.

On the other hand, evolution was solving a very constrained problem. It had to build everything incrementally, every intermediate step had to be viable, and it had to self-assemble from a single cell using whatever chemistry was available. It couldn't just decide to use metal or wheels or a separate power plant. So in some ways the comparison is unfair to evolution. It produced systems that are extraordinarily good given those constraints, and we often beat them by sidestepping the constraints rather than by being cleverer within them.

What I find most useful is asking what the comparison is actually supposed to tell you. If the question is "how long until our technology matches some biological capability," the historical pattern is informative. For flight, locomotion, and vision, the first human systems that matched biology were usually much worse on some dimensions, like energy efficiency or robustness, but better on others, like raw speed or scale. Then over time we tend to pull ahead on most dimensions. Planes don't fly like birds, and they're worse at plenty of things birds do, but nobody thinks birds are winning.

For AI and the brain, I think the most relevant takeaway is that the brain gives a rough existence proof and a loose anchor on how much computation might be needed. It's probably not a tight bound. We'll likely get there with systems that are less efficient in some ways but compensate with more compute, more data, and the ability to copy and scale in ways biology can't. So I'd treat biological comparisons as useful order-of-magnitude anchors, while being skeptical of anyone who uses them to argue we're either nearly there or impossibly far away.

r001.rationale: The response compares particular capabilities such as flight, locomotion, and vision, but does not identify a shared functional need as the basis for making the comparison fair.

r002.rationale: It explains that human technology can gain advantages by bypassing evolutionary constraints, and gives examples such as planes offering greater speed or scale than birds.

r003.rationale: It does not explain wheeled transport’s advantage by noting that animals cannot pave roads.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this comes up a lot in the context of trying to forecast AI, where people want to say something like, "Evolution took billions of years and enormous amounts of compute to produce the human brain, so we should expect it to be really hard for humans to replicate that." And I think the comparison is interesting but you have to be pretty careful about what you're actually comparing.

The basic thing I'd say is that evolution is a very different kind of optimizer than human engineering, and it's not obvious in which direction that cuts. On one hand, evolution has had a tremendous amount of compute to work with, it's been running experiments in parallel across trillions of organisms for a very long time. On the other hand, evolution is a really dumb optimizer in a bunch of ways. It's doing something like hill climbing on a very noisy, very sparse signal, it can't look ahead, it can't do the kind of deliberate design that engineers do, and it's constrained in all sorts of ways by the path it took to get where it is. It can't just rip out the retina and redesign it the right way around.

So when people look at examples where human technology beat biology, like flight or solar panels, they'll say, "Look, we did in a century what evolution couldn't do in hundreds of millions of years." And I think that's right in some sense, but it's also partly that we were optimizing for a different objective. Evolution wasn't trying to make the fastest flying thing, it was trying to make a thing that could reproduce, and a jet engine is just not something you can evolve incrementally by making a bird slightly better at reproducing. Similarly, when people point at areas where biology is still way ahead, like the energy efficiency of the brain, or the brain's sample efficiency, I think you want to ask whether that's because the problem is actually hard or because we just haven't put in the effort yet, or because we've been optimizing for a different thing.

The way I'd try to actually use these comparisons is more quantitative. If you want to say "AI is going to be hard because brains are hard," you want to try to estimate how much optimization evolution actually did on the relevant thing, in a currency that's comparable to the optimization we're doing. And when you try to do that, I think it tends to look like evolution did a lot of work in some respects, like a lot of total compute, but that a lot of that compute was wasted in the sense that it wasn't going toward the thing we care about. Most of the organisms in that history weren't doing anything that looks like cognition, and even for the ones that were, the selection pressure on cognition specifically was a pretty small part of the total.

And then separately there's the question of the learning that happens within a lifetime, which is a thing that evolution was selecting for rather than doing directly. A lot of what makes a human smart isn't that evolution found the weights, it's that evolution found a learning algorithm and some priors, and then the human brain does the rest with a lifetime of data. So the relevant comparison for AI is often less "can we match billions of years of evolution" and more "can we match the within-lifetime learning plus a reasonable amount of search over architectures," which seems like a much more approachable problem.

I'd also say there's a selection effect in which comparisons people bring up. We're more likely to notice the cases where human technology clearly won, because those are the cases where there's a product, and the cases where biology is clearly ahead, because those are the cases that are interesting puzzles. The messy middle, where we're sort of comparable in different ways, doesn't make for a good story. So I'd be somewhat skeptical of any argument that leans too heavily on a couple of cherry-picked examples in either direction.

I guess overall my view is that these comparisons are useful mostly for calibration. They give you some anchors on how much compute it might take, or on whether a given problem is one where you'd expect deliberate design to beat incremental search. But I wouldn't want to put too much weight on any one of them, and I especially wouldn't want to take "evolution couldn't do it" as strong evidence that humans can't either, because evolution couldn't do a lot of things that turned out to be pretty easy once you could actually think about the problem.

r001.rationale: The response says comparisons should account for whether humans and evolution were optimizing for the same objective, and recommends comparing optimization on the relevant thing. This communicates the need for a shared target.

r002.rationale: It offers objective mismatch as a partial explanation for examples such as flight, but emphasizes that the comparison is complicated and that the causes vary. It does not suggest that human advantages generally have a straightforward explanation.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss wheeled transport, roads, or animals’ inability to pave their environment.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends a lot on what you’re trying to infer from the comparison. Evolution has had an enormous amount of time to optimize biological systems, but it’s also operating under a very different set of constraints. So if you say, “Our technology doesn’t match biology on this dimension,” that’s useful evidence, but it’s not necessarily evidence that humans are bad at designing things.

For example, a bird has to grow itself, find its own fuel, repair damage, and reproduce. An airplane gets to rely on this huge industrial infrastructure. If you compare just how fast they fly, the airplane wins, but you’ve left out a lot of what the bird is doing. Conversely, if you compare their ability to reproduce, you’re asking the airplane to do something it wasn’t designed for.

The thing I find most compelling about biology is that it gives you an existence proof. We know that a system can perform human-level cognition using roughly the resources a brain uses, because evolution produced one. That doesn’t tell you how hard it will be for us to build something comparable, or whether we’ll use the same approach. But it does tell you that the capability is physically possible. I’d put much more weight on that than on a general claim that human engineering is better or worse than evolution.

r001.rationale: It discusses comparing performance dimensions and constraints, but does not identify a shared functional need as the basis for a fair comparison.

r002.rationale: It says an airplane’s advantage in speed reflects different constraints and infrastructure, but does not claim that technology’s major advantages over evolution generally have straightforward explanations.

r003.rationale: It gives a bird-versus-airplane example, but says nothing about wheeled road transport or animals’ inability to pave their environment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what comparison you’re trying to make. If you’re asking whether humans are better engineers than evolution, you have to account for the resources involved. Evolution has been running an enormous search over a very long time. On the other hand, it’s operating under constraints that are quite different from ours. Every intermediate organism has to survive and reproduce, and evolution can’t step back and decide to redesign the whole system from scratch.

So when we look at something like the brain, I think it’s reasonable to take it as an existence proof: you can produce intelligent behavior with this amount of energy and this amount of physical hardware. But it’s much less clear that it tells you the best we could do, or how hard it will be for us to get there. We can use different materials, copy successful designs, and optimize directly for the thing we care about.

The comparison is useful, but you need to specify what you’re holding fixed. Matching biology’s performance, matching its energy efficiency, and matching the amount of search that went into producing it are very different challenges.

r002.rationale: It discusses different resources and constraints, but does not suggest that human technology’s large advantages over evolution generally have straightforward explanations.
